identity.title: What's In My Human Feedback? Learning Interpretable Descriptions of Preference Data

problem.claim: Practitioners need to understand what human-feedback data encodes so they can interpret and use it safely.

gap.claim: Automatically extracting relevant preference features without pre-specified hypotheses remains challenging.

contributions.claim: Introduces WIMHF, which uses sparse autoencoders to explain preference data.
Characterizes both the preferences a dataset can measure and those annotators actually express.
Uses learned interpretable features for data curation and annotator-specific personalization.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present WIMHF as a human-centered method for analyzing preference data through sparse-autoencoder-derived, interpretable features.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Across 7 datasets, a small number of human-interpretable features account for most of the preference-prediction signal achieved by black-box models.
The analysis reports strong dataset-context differences: Reddit users prefer informality and jokes, whereas HH-RLHF and PRISM annotators disprefer them.

The authors report that relabeling harmful Arena examples produces a +37% safety gain with no cost to general performance, and that annotator-specific feature weights improve preference prediction on Community Alignment.

narrative_sequence.summary: Human feedback can change language models unpredictably, while its encoded preferences are difficult to understand.
Existing studies examine selected attributes, but hypothesis-free feature extraction remains challenging.
WIMHF applies sparse autoencoders and separates measurable dataset preferences from expressed annotator preferences.
Across seven datasets, sparse interpretable features capture most black-box prediction signal and expose diverse, context-dependent and potentially unsafe preferences.
The features support safety-oriented data curation and fine-grained personalization.

source_observation.claim: The abstract distinguishes what a dataset is capable of measuring from what annotators actually express, then demonstrates both curation and personalization uses.

lessons.interpretation: Separating measurement capacity from observed behavior can connect interpretability analysis to concrete operational decisions.
lessons.application: When presenting a preference-data method, explicitly report these two layers and map each to a downstream intervention.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when the data cannot support a meaningful distinction between measurement capacity and annotator behavior.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify how features, prediction signal, safety gains, or preference-prediction improvements were measured.
The +37% safety result lacks baseline, evaluation scope, statistical uncertainty, and relabeling details.
The abstract does not establish whether the reported findings generalize beyond the named datasets.
